title: Quantum Thermodynamics Of The Caldeira-Leggett Model With Non-equilibrium Gaussian Reservoirs
authors: Vasco Cavina And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2136 (2026).

We introduce a non-equilibrium version of the Caldeira-Leggett model in which a quantum particle is strongly coupled to a set of engineered reservoirs. The reservoirs are composed by collections of squeezed and displaced thermal modes, in contrast to the standard case in which the modes are assumed to be at equilibrium. The model proves to be very versatile. Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs can be used to generate an effective time dependence in the system Hamiltonian and can be identified as sources of pure work. In the case of squeezing, the time dependence is stochastic and breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, this can be reconciled with the second law of thermodynamics by correctly accounting for the energy used to generate the initial non-equilibrium conditions. To go beyond the average description and compute the full heat statistics, we treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour. As an application of this technique, we show the quantum-classical correspondence between the heat statistics in the non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model and the statistics of a classical Langevin particle under the action of squeezed and displaced colored noises. Finally, we discuss thermodynamic symmetries of the heat generating function, proving a fluctuation theorem for the energy balance and showing that the conservation of energy at the trajectory level emerges in the classical limit.

.
tldr: This paper extends the Caldeira-Leggett model to non-equilibrium Gaussian reservoirs, enabling the study of quantum thermodynamics with strong coupling and providing a framework for heat statistics and fluctuation theorems.
motivation: Standard quantum thermodynamics often assumes equilibrium reservoirs, but many realistic systems involve non-equilibrium conditions. The authors aim to develop a versatile model that captures strong coupling and non-equilibrium effects.
method: They introduce a non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model with squeezed and displaced thermal reservoirs, treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour, and compute full heat statistics.
result: The model generates effective time dependence and pure work from displacement, while squeezing breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation. A fluctuation theorem for energy balance is proven, and quantum-classical correspondence is shown.
conclusion: The work provides a powerful tool for analyzing quantum thermodynamics in non-equilibrium settings, with implications for heat engines and information processing.

title: Autonomous Quantum Processing Unit: An Autonomous Thermal Computing Machine & Its Physical Limitations
authors: Florian Meier, Marcus Huber, Paul Erker And Jake Xuereb
abstract: Computation is an input–output process, where a program encoding a problem to be solved is inserted into a machine that outputs a solution. Quantum computation conventionally relies on classical, external control outside the quantum computer to execute a program, obscuring computational and thermodynamic resources required. To understand the fundamental limits of computation, however, it is pivotal to work with a fully self-contained description of a quantum computation modeling the resources on the same footing as the computation itself. By developing a framework that we dub the autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) we model quantum computation in the framework of autonomous thermal machines. Consisting of an internal quantum timekeeping mechanism, instruction register and memory system the aQPU allows investigating relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed and fidelity of a desired quantum computation.
tldr: The paper introduces an autonomous Quantum Processing Unit (aQPU) as a thermal machine that self-contains all computational and thermodynamic resources, enabling the study of fundamental limits of quantum computation.
motivation: Conventional quantum computation relies on external classical control, obscuring the true thermodynamic and computational costs. A fully self-contained model is needed to understand fundamental limits.
method: The authors develop a framework modeling quantum computation as an autonomous thermal machine, incorporating an internal quantum clock, instruction register, and memory system.
result: The aQPU framework allows investigation of relationships between thermodynamic cost, complexity, speed, and fidelity of quantum computations.
conclusion: This work provides a foundation for analyzing the physical limitations of quantum computation from a thermodynamic perspective, bridging quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture linking energy fluctuations to geometric length in state preparation, showing that curvature of control spaces can lead to violations.
motivation: Understanding fundamental speed limits in quantum state preparation is crucial for quantum control and thermodynamics. The conjecture by Bukov et al. suggested a lower bound on energy fluctuations based on geometric length, which if true would have deep implications.
method: The authors analyze the geometry of state preparation protocols using the Fubini-Study metric and consider control spaces with extrinsic curvature. They construct explicit counterexamples in qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems.
result: They demonstrate that the conjectured bound can be violated when the accessible parameter space is curved, meaning energy fluctuations can be smaller than the minimal geometric length would suggest.
conclusion: The geometric speed limit is not universal; curvature of control spaces must be accounted for. This refines our understanding of thermodynamic costs in quantum control.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper analytically and numerically studies non-Markovian cooperative radiation in two-level atoms coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing superabsorption and critical regimes.
motivation: Understanding cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations is crucial for quantum information processing with hybrid systems.
method: The authors derive an exact analytical solution for two emitters and use a numerically exact method for larger ensembles to characterize the transition from Markovian to non-Markovian dynamics.
result: They identify three regimes: Markovian superradiance, non-Markovian superabsorption, and a critical pulsed regime; superradiant peak intensity scaling degrades with system size, approaching subquadratic in the perfect cavity limit.
conclusion: Environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity, and spontaneous superabsorption is a distinct non-Markovian cooperative phenomenon.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: Proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive.
method: The authors propose a scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and heuristic arguments, proving bounds on the adversary's success probability.
result: They prove a quadratic convergence bound for the adversary's success probability for up to 5 keys, and provide numerical and asymptotic upper bounds.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence that unconditional uncloneable encryption is achievable, advancing the foundations of quantum uncloneability.

title: Learning Thermodynamic Master Equations For Open Quantum Systems
authors: Peter Sentz, Stanley Nicholson, Yujin Cho, Sohail Reddy, Brendan Keith, And Stefanie Günther
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2151 (2026).

The characterization of Hamiltonians and other components of open quantum dynamical systems plays a crucial role in quantum computing and other applications. Scientific machine learning techniques have been applied to this problem in a variety of ways, including by modeling with deep neural networks. However, the majority of mathematical models describing open quantum systems are linear, and the natural nonlinearities in learnable models have not been incorporated using physical principles. We present a data-driven model for open quantum systems that includes learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms. The trained model is interpretable, as it directly estimates the system Hamiltonian and linear components of coupling to the environment. We validate the model on synthetic two and three-level data, as well as experimental two-level data collected from a quantum device at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.

.
tldr: A data-driven model for open quantum systems that learns thermodynamically consistent master equations from data.
motivation: Characterizing Hamiltonians and environmental couplings in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum computing, but existing machine learning approaches often lack thermodynamic consistency.
method: The authors propose a neural network model that incorporates learnable, thermodynamically consistent terms, directly estimating the system Hamiltonian and linear coupling components.
result: The model is validated on synthetic two- and three-level systems and experimental two-level data from a quantum device, demonstrating accurate and interpretable recovery of system parameters.
conclusion: The approach provides a physically principled, interpretable machine learning framework for modeling open quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum device characterization and control.

title: Entanglement In The Dicke Subspace
authors: Aabhas Gulati, Ion Nechita, And Clément Pellegrini
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2150 (2026).

We provide a complete mathematical theory for the entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states. These quantum states form an important subclass of bosonic states arising in the study of indistinguishable particles. We introduce a tensor-based parametrization where the diagonal entries of these states are encoded as a symmetric tensor, enabling a direct translation between entanglement properties and well-studied convex cones of tensors. Our results bridge multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and the theory of completely positive and copositive tensors. This dictionary maps separability to completely positive tensors, the PPT property to moment tensors, entanglement witnesses to copositive tensors, and decomposable witnesses to sum of squares tensors. We establish that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension [MATH] and [MATH] parties, disproving a recent conjecture. We also show that, for mixtures of Dicke states, the PPT condition with respect to the most balanced bipartition implies all other PPT conditions. We further connect bosonic extendibility of mixtures of Dicke states to the duals of known hierarchies for non-negative polynomials, such as the ones by Reznick and Polya. We thus provide semidefinite programming relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

.
tldr: Provides a complete mathematical theory for entanglement of mixtures of Dicke states, linking separability and PPT properties to convex cones of tensors.
motivation: Understanding entanglement in bosonic systems is important for quantum information, but mixtures of Dicke states lacked a unified mathematical framework.
method: Introduces a tensor-based parametrization where diagonal entries are encoded as symmetric tensors, mapping entanglement properties to well-studied convex cones (completely positive, copositive, moment tensors).
result: Establishes that PPT entanglement exists for all multipartite systems with local dimension ≥3 and ≥3 parties, disproving a recent conjecture; shows PPT condition for the most balanced bipartition implies all others; connects bosonic extendibility to hierarchies for non-negative polynomials.
conclusion: The work bridges multipartite entanglement theory with semialgebraic geometry and provides SDP relaxations for separability and entanglement testing in the Dicke subspace.

title: Measuring Rényi Entropy With An Echo Protocol
authors: Yi-Neng Zhou, Robin Löwenberg, And Julian Sonner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2146 (2026).

We present efficient and practical protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy, whose exponential is known as the purity. Our approach is based on expressing the purity in terms of transition probabilities generated by an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, making it applicable to quantum many-body systems. Notably, our approach does not rely on random-noise averaging, a feature that can be extended to protocols to measure out-of-time-order correlation functions, as we demonstrate. By way of example, we show that our protocols can be practically implemented in superconducting qubit-based platforms, as well as in cavity-QED trapped ultra-cold gases.

.
tldr: Presents efficient echo-based protocols to measure the second Rényi entropy (purity) in quantum many-body systems without random-noise averaging.
motivation: Measuring Rényi entropy is crucial for characterizing entanglement and quantum correlations, but existing methods often require random averaging or are inefficient.
method: The purity is expressed in terms of transition probabilities from an echo-type forward-backward evolution sequence, avoiding random-noise averaging; the protocol is extended to out-of-time-order correlators.
result: The protocols are shown to be practically implementable on superconducting qubit platforms and cavity-QED trapped ultracold gases.
conclusion: Provides efficient, noise-avoiding measurement schemes for Rényi entropy, advancing experimental quantum information processing.

title: Measurement Incompatibility And Quantum Steering Via Linear Programming
authors: Lucas E. A. Porto, Sébastien Designolle, Sebastian Pokutta, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2141 (2026).

The problem of deciding whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable is known to be equivalent to determining whether a quantum assemblage is unsteerable. This problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). However, the number of variables and constraints in such a formulation grows exponentially with the number of measurements, rendering it intractable for large measurement sets. In this work, we circumvent this problem by transforming the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that compute upper and lower bounds on the incompatibility robustness with a complexity that grows polynomially in the number of measurements. The hierarchy is guaranteed to converge and it can be applied to arbitrary measurements – including non-projective POVMs (Positive Operator-Valued Measures) – in arbitrary dimensions. While convergence becomes impractical in high dimensions, in the case of qubits our method reliably provides accurate upper and lower bounds for the incompatibility robustness of sets with several hundred measurements in a short time using a standard laptop. We also apply our methods to qutrits, obtaining non-trivial upper and lower bounds in scenarios that are otherwise intractable using the standard SDP approach, although such bounds are significantly looser than the ones obtained in the qubit case. Finally, we show how our methods can be used to construct local hidden state models for states (i.e., to prove that a state cannot lead to steering under any possible local measurements), or conversely, to certify that a given state exhibits steering; for two-qubit quantum states, our approach is comparable to, and in some cases outperforms, the current best methods.

.
tldr: This paper transforms the semidefinite program for joint measurability and steering into a hierarchy of linear programs, enabling efficient computation of bounds for large measurement sets.
motivation: Determining whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable or a state is steerable is computationally intractable for large measurement sets due to exponential growth of variables in the standard SDP formulation.
method: The authors reformulate the SDP as a hierarchy of linear programs that provide upper and lower bounds on incompatibility robustness, with polynomial complexity in the number of measurements.
result: For qubits, the method yields accurate bounds for sets with hundreds of measurements quickly on a laptop; for qutrits, non-trivial bounds are obtained where SDP is intractable. The approach also constructs local hidden state models or certifies steering for two-qubit states.
conclusion: The linear programming hierarchy offers a practical tool for analyzing measurement incompatibility and quantum steering in large scenarios, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: Tight bounds for quantum phase estimation with advice states, including nearly matching lower bounds and a resolution of an open problem.
motivation: Phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine, but its cost with advice states (e.g., eigenstate copies) was not tightly characterized. Understanding this helps optimize quantum algorithms.
method: Uses the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials to derive lower bounds, and provides matching upper bounds via explicit algorithms.
result: Characterizes the cost for all parameter regimes, showing that few advice copies are not significantly better than none, and many copies do not reduce cost much. Also gives a tight bound for error probability reduction.
conclusion: Provides a complete complexity picture for phase estimation with advice, resolving an open question about the Unitary recurrence time problem.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity, showing that stabilizer states with maximal Wigner negativity achieve maximal violation.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because stabilizer states and Clifford operators do not produce violations for qudits as they do for qubits.
method: The authors define a Bell operator using correlations related to Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized π/8 gate, and analyze its properties.
result: A specific stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality, and the Bell operator quantifies both singlet fraction and volume of Wigner negativity.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems, and the proposed inequality provides a new tool for studying nonlocality and contextuality in higher dimensions.

title: Distributing Graph States With A Photon-weaving Quantum Server
authors: Daniel Bhatti And Kenneth Goodenough
abstract: One of the key aims of quantum networks is the efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states among end users. While various architectures have been proposed, each comes with distinct advantages and limitations. Many designs depend on long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates, which, while powerful, introduce considerable cost and technical challenges. Experimentally cheaper alternatives that circumvent these constraints are often limited to specific types of entanglement and a specific number of users. Here, we present an experiment-friendly quantum server that relies only on linear optical elements, offering a flexible approach to multipartite entanglement distribution. Our so-called photon-weaving quantum server can generate and distribute one of several locally nonequivalent graph states, including Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states, as well as path, cycle, and caterpillar graph states. This is achieved through two distinct fusion protocols, i.e. multiphoton graph-state fusion (graph-state weaving) and multiphoton GHZ-state fusion (GHZ-state weaving), and can readily be implemented.
tldr: Proposes an experiment-friendly quantum server using linear optics to distribute various graph states among end users.
motivation: Efficient distribution of multipartite entangled states is key for quantum networks, but existing architectures often require costly long-lived quantum memories and deterministic gates.
method: The server uses two fusion protocols—graph-state weaving and GHZ-state weaving—with only linear optical elements to generate and distribute graph states like GHZ, path, cycle, and caterpillar states.
result: The photon-weaving server can generate several locally nonequivalent graph states, offering flexibility in entanglement distribution without the need for quantum memories or deterministic gates.
conclusion: This approach provides a practical, scalable solution for multipartite entanglement distribution in quantum networks, reducing experimental complexity.

title: Phase-controlled Thermal Amplification In A Quantum Thermal Transistor
authors: Xiaoyun Wang And Dazhi Xu
abstract: We investigate phase-controlled heat transport in a quantum thermal transistor composed of three coupled two-level systems, each connected to an independent thermal reservoir. Using a nonsecular Redfield master equation, we show that a gauge-invariant phase in the triangular coupling loop provides an efficient control knob beyond reservoir temperatures: at fixed temperature bias, tuning the phase strongly modulates the steady-state heat currents and can generate pronounced thermal amplification, whereby a small variation of the control current induces large changes in the currents at the other two terminals. We further analyze how the amplification depends on the reservoir temperature as well as on the intersystem couplings, identifying regimes of enhanced performance. To clarify the underlying mechanism, we develop a complementary weak-coupling theory based on a local Lindblad equation and second-order cumulant expansion. This analysis shows that the phase first enters the exchange coherences and is then transferred to the populations through loop interference, while the heat currents are dominated by the resulting population corrections. Our results establish phase engineering as a flexible route to regulating heat flow and thermal amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.
tldr: A quantum thermal transistor using three coupled two-level systems demonstrates phase-controlled heat amplification.
motivation: To explore phase engineering as a control knob for heat flow in quantum thermal devices, beyond temperature bias.
method: Uses a nonsecular Redfield master equation and a local Lindblad equation with second-order cumulant expansion to model heat transport.
result: Tuning the gauge-invariant phase strongly modulates steady-state heat currents and enables thermal amplification.
conclusion: Phase control offers a flexible route to regulate heat flow and amplification in multi-terminal quantum thermal devices.

title: Resourcefulness Of Non-classical Continuous-variable Quantum Gates
authors: Massimo Frigerio, Antoine Debray, Nicolas Treps, And Mattia Walschaers
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2155 (2026).

In continuous-variable quantum computation, identifying key elements that enable a quantum computational advantage is a long-standing issue. Starting from the standard results on the necessity of Wigner negativity, we develop a comprehensive and versatile approach in which the techniques of [MATH]-ordered quasiprobabilities are exploited to provide rigorous statements on the simulability of photonic quantum circuits consisting of previously characterized gates and thereby identifying the contribution of each quantum gate to the potential achievement of quantum computational advantage. This is achieved by means of an analysis of the so-called transfer function, allowing us to highlight the resourcefulness of a gate set. As such this technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variables quantum circuits, while also constraining the tolerable amount of losses above which any potential quantum advantage can be ruled out. We use [MATH]-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space to capture the non-classical features in the protocol, and focus our technique entirely on the ordering parameter [MATH]. This allows us to highlight the resourcefulness and robustness to loss of a universal set of unitary gates comprising three distinct Gaussian gates and any non-Gaussian unitary gate, providing important insight on the role of non-Gaussianity.

.
tldr: Develops a comprehensive approach using s-ordered quasiprobabilities to quantify the resourcefulness of non-classical continuous-variable quantum gates for achieving quantum computational advantage.
motivation: Identifying key elements enabling quantum computational advantage in continuous-variable quantum computation is a long-standing issue; the paper aims to provide rigorous simulability criteria and highlight the role of non-Gaussianity.
method: Uses s-ordered quasiprobability distributions on phase-space and the transfer function to analyze the resourcefulness of a gate set, focusing on the ordering parameter s to capture non-classical features.
result: Provides rigorous statements on simulability of photonic quantum circuits, identifies the contribution of each quantum gate to potential quantum advantage, and constrains the tolerable amount of losses above which advantage is ruled out.
conclusion: The technique can be straightforwardly applied to current continuous-variable quantum circuits and offers important insight into the role of non-Gaussianity and robustness to loss.

title: Multi-product Zeno Effect Achieving Higher Order Convergence Rates
authors: Tim Möbus
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2148 (2026).

The quantum Zeno effect is a fundamental mechanism for implementing the effective dynamics of projected Hamiltonian and Lindbladian systems. It approximates the target projected evolution by interleaving Hamiltonian or Lindblad dynamics with quantum operations associated with the desired subspace. In contrast to the related Trotter product formula, the best-known convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect is typically limited to order [MATH]. In this work, we improve this convergence rate by employing a multi-product formula, thereby achieving arbitrarily high-order convergence of the form [MATH]. This yields an improved approximation scheme for Zeno-like expectation values via an efficient post-processing method. The approach combines a modified Chernoff lemma, an adapted Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation. We illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and also consider the broader class of systems governed by the Bang-Bang decoupling method.

.
tldr: This paper improves the convergence rate of the quantum Zeno effect to arbitrarily high order using multi-product formulas, with applications to projected dynamics and Bang-Bang decoupling.
motivation: The standard quantum Zeno effect has limited convergence rate (order 1), which restricts its efficiency in approximating projected dynamics. Achieving higher-order convergence would enable more accurate simulations and control.
method: The authors combine a modified Chernoff lemma, Dunford-Segal approximation, holomorphic functional calculus, and Chebyshev interpolation to construct a multi-product formula that yields arbitrarily high-order convergence for the Zeno effect.
result: They demonstrate that the multi-product Zeno effect achieves convergence rates of order k for any integer k, and illustrate the method with the bosonic cat code and Bang-Bang decoupling.
conclusion: The multi-product approach significantly enhances the quantum Zeno effect's convergence, providing a powerful tool for quantum simulation and control of open systems.

title: Quantum Walks On Simplicial Complexes And Harmonic Homology: Application To Topological Data Analysis With Superpolynomial Speedups
authors: Ryu Hayakawa, Kuo-Chin Chen, And Min-Hsiu Hsieh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2138 (2026).

This work investigates whether quantum walks on simplicial complexes exhibit quantum advantages. We introduce a novel quantum walk that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, a key object reflecting the topology of the simplicial complex. We construct a unitary encoding projecting onto the kernel of the Laplacian, representing the harmonic cycles in the complex's homology. Our efficient construction of quantum walk unitaries for clique complexes paves the way for exploring higher-order interactions within topological structures. Our construction requires [MATH] gates, where [MATH] is the number of vertices, [MATH] is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian, and [MATH] is the projection error. Our results indicate apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup with quantum walks, without quantum oracles, provided the spectral gap of the Laplacian is inverse-polynomially bounded and efficient simplex sampling is available. Crucially, the walk operates on a state space encompassing both positively and negatively oriented simplices, effectively doubling its size compared to unoriented approaches. Through coherent interference of these paired simplices, we are able to successfully encode the combinatorial Laplacian, which would otherwise be impossible. This is our major technical contribution. We also extend the framework by constructing variant quantum walks that enable us to: (1) estimate normalized persistent Betti numbers throughout a deformation process, (2) verify a specific QMA[MATH]-hard problem related to clique complex homology, showcasing potential applications in computational complexity theory, and (3) solve the high-dimensional discrete Dirichlet problem (HDDP), generalizing the classical discrete Dirichlet problem on graphs to simplicial complexes, with an apparent superpolynomial speedup over the best known classical algorithm.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a quantum walk on simplicial complexes that encodes the combinatorial Laplacian, enabling superpolynomial speedups for topological data analysis and related problems.
motivation: Quantum walks on graphs have shown advantages, but extending them to simplicial complexes could unlock new quantum algorithms for topological data analysis and homology computation.
method: The authors construct a unitary encoding of the combinatorial Laplacian using a quantum walk on oriented simplices, with coherent interference between positive and negative orientations to encode the Laplacian.
result: The construction achieves apparent superpolynomial quantum speedup for estimating Betti numbers, verifying a QMA-hard problem, and solving the high-dimensional Dirichlet problem, assuming an inverse-polynomial spectral gap and efficient simplex sampling.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that quantum walks on simplicial complexes can provide significant quantum advantages for topological data analysis without relying on quantum oracles, opening new avenues for quantum algorithms in topology.

title: Heralded Ultrafast Generation Of Macroscopic Quantum States In Matter With Bright Squeezed Vacuum Light
authors: Shohei Imai
abstract: We show that bright squeezed vacuum light, combined with a single-shot quadrature measurement of the post-interaction light, enables the ultrafast generation of macroscopic quantum states in matter. Although in the weak-coupling regime multiphoton quantum light leaves the unconditional matter state as a classical mixture due to light–matter entanglement, quadrature-based heralding prepares the matter in a Gaussian-weighted quantum superposition of laser-driven matter states. For an ensemble of resonantly electric-dipole-coupled two-level systems, this heralding dynamics acts as a Gaussian filter with respect to the electric polarization, with brighter squeezed-vacuum light accelerating the preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state. Counter-rotating terms further drive a stroboscopic transition from this Dicke state to a cat-like state. Our results open a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter with strong-field quantum light.
tldr: This paper proposes a method to generate macroscopic quantum states in matter by heralding on quadrature measurements of bright squeezed vacuum light.
motivation: Generating macroscopic quantum states is challenging due to decoherence; ultrafast optical methods offer a potential route but typically require strong coupling. The authors aim to use bright squeezed vacuum light to achieve this in the weak-coupling regime.
method: They consider an ensemble of two-level systems coupled to bright squeezed vacuum light. After interaction, a single-shot quadrature measurement on the light heralds the matter state, which becomes a Gaussian-weighted superposition of laser-driven states.
result: The heralding acts as a Gaussian filter on the electric polarization, accelerating preparation of the zero-eigenvalue Dicke state. Counter-rotating terms can further drive a transition to a cat-like state.
conclusion: This work opens a route to ultrafast engineering of macroscopic quantum matter using strong-field quantum light, relevant for quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: A sample-optimal protocol for quantum measurement tomography using projected least squares estimation.
motivation: Existing quantum measurement tomography protocols are computationally expensive or suboptimal in sample complexity; a practical, sample-optimal method is needed.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the estimate onto the set of valid POVMs.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both worst-case and average-case distance, with matching lower bounds established.
conclusion: Projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal and computationally efficient, with rigorous error guarantees.

title: Non-Markovian Quantum Mpemba Effect In Strongly Correlated Quantum Dots
authors: Yuandong Wang And Jianhua Wei
abstract: Harnessing non-Markovian effects has emerged as a resource for quantum control, where a structured environment can act as a quantum memory. We investigate the quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium steady states in strongly correlated quantum dot systems. The distance between quantum states is quantified using the Bures metric, which endows the space of reduced density matrices with a Riemannian geometric structure. Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, we demonstrate a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) arising from non-Markovianity. Unlike previous studies centered on non-interacting limits, we reveal a distinct non-Markovian QME uniquely driven by the initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance. Furthermore, by tracking the dynamical evolution in the generalized Bloch parameter space, we uncover an intrinsic QME. This trajectory-dependent analysis provides a rigorous geometric perspective on the circuitous relaxation pathways driven by Kondo correlations. Our results underscore the critical role of memory effects in quantum quench dynamics and suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect in strongly correlated quantum dots, driven by Kondo correlations and memory effects.
motivation: Understanding anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems is crucial for quantum control; the quantum Mpemba effect offers a new perspective on non-equilibrium dynamics.
method: Using the numerically exact hierarchical equations of motion method, the authors study quench dynamics from specific initial states to equilibrium, quantifying state distance via the Bures metric and analyzing trajectories in generalized Bloch parameter space.
result: They reveal a distinct non-Markovian quantum Mpemba effect uniquely driven by initial-state-dependent formation of the many-body Kondo resonance, and uncover an intrinsic QME through geometric analysis.
conclusion: Memory effects play a critical role in quantum quench dynamics, and the findings suggest new pathways for controlling anomalous relaxation in open quantum systems.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: Introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a necessary and sufficient condition for robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements.
motivation: Previous characterizations like GFlow and Pauli Flow were insufficient for MBQC involving Pauli measurements; a complete characterization was needed.
method: Extends Pauli Flow to Shadow Pauli Flow, proving its necessity and sufficiency for robust determinism, and provides a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is both necessary and sufficient for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, capturing all possible correction strategies.
conclusion: This work provides a complete graphical characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, enabling efficient verification of deterministic computations.

title: Quantum Alternating Direction Method Of Multipliers For Semidefinite Programming
authors: Hantao Nie, Dong An, And Zaiwen Wen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2154 (2026).

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a fundamental convex optimization problem with wide-ranging applications. However, solving large-scale instances remains computationally challenging due to the high cost of solving linear systems and performing eigenvalue decompositions. In this paper, we present a quantum alternating direction method of multipliers (QADMM) for SDPs, building on recent advances in quantum computing. An inexact ADMM framework is developed, which tolerates errors in the iterates arising from block-encoding approximation and quantum measurement. Within this robust scheme, we design a polynomial proximal operator to address the semidefinite conic constraints and apply the quantum singular value transformation to accelerate the most costly projection updates. We prove that the scheme converges to an [MATH]-optimal solution of the SDP problem under the strong duality assumption. A detailed complexity analysis shows that the QADMM algorithm achieves favorable scaling with respect to dimension compared to the classical ADMM algorithm and quantum interior point methods, highlighting its potential for solving large-scale SDPs.

.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for semidefinite programming using ADMM and quantum singular value transformation, achieving better dimension scaling than classical methods.
motivation: Solving large-scale SDPs is computationally expensive due to linear systems and eigenvalue decompositions; quantum computing offers potential speedups.
method: Develops an inexact ADMM framework tolerant to errors from block-encoding and measurement, uses polynomial proximal operator for semidefinite constraints, and applies quantum singular value transformation for projection updates.
result: Proves convergence to an optimal solution under strong duality and shows favorable dimension scaling compared to classical ADMM and quantum interior point methods.
conclusion: QADMM is a promising quantum algorithm for large-scale SDPs, though practical implementation depends on future quantum hardware.
keywords: quantum alternating direction method of multipliers

title: Exploring Imaginary Coordinates: Disparity In The Shape Of Quantum State Space In Even And Odd Dimensions
authors: Simon Morelli, Santiago Llorens, And Jens Siewert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2153 (2026).

The state of a finite-dimensional quantum system is described by a density matrix that can be decomposed into a real diagonal, a real off-diagonal and and an imaginary off-diagonal part. The latter plays a peculiar role. While it is intuitively clear that some of the imaginary coordinates cannot have the same extension as their real counterparts the precise relation is not obvious. We give a complete characterization of the constraints in terms of tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates. Our description entails a three-dimensional Bloch ball-type model for the state space. We uncover a surprising qualitative difference for the state-space boundaries in even and odd dimensions.

.
tldr: This paper fully characterizes the constraints on imaginary Bloch coordinates for finite-dimensional quantum states, revealing a parity-dependent shape of the state space.
motivation: Understanding the geometry of quantum state space is fundamental to quantum information theory, and the role of imaginary coordinates was not fully characterized.
method: The authors derive tight inequalities for real and imaginary Bloch-type coordinates, constructing a three-dimensional Bloch ball model for the state space.
result: They find a surprising qualitative difference in the state-space boundaries between even and odd dimensions.
conclusion: The work provides a complete geometric description of the constraints on imaginary coordinates, which may impact entanglement theory and quantum state discrimination.

title: On The Addressability Problem On Css Codes
authors: Jérôme Guyot And Samuel Jaques
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2145 (2026).

Recent discoveries in asymptotically good quantum codes have intensified research on their application in quantum computation and fault-tolerant operations. This study focuses on the addressability problem within CSS codes: we ask what circuits might implement logical gates on strict subsets of logical qubits. With some notion of fault-tolerance, we prove several impossibility results: for CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address a logical [MATH], [MATH], [MATH], or [MATH] to any non-empty strict subset of logical qubits using a circuit made only from 1-local Clifford gates. Furthermore, we show that one cannot permute the logical qubits in a code purely by permuting the physical qubits, if the rate of the code is (asymptotically) greater than 1/3 and the distance is at least 3. We can show a similar no-go result for [MATH]s and [MATH]s between two such high-rate codes, albeit under a more restrictive assumption on the circuit, which we call "global" (though recent addressable CCZ gates use global circuits). This work pioneers the study of distance-preserving addressability in quantum codes, mainly by considering automorphisms of the code. This perspective offers new insights and potential directions for future research. We argue that studying this trade off between addressability and efficiency of the codes is essential to understand better how to do efficient quantum computation.

.
tldr: This paper proves impossibility results for addressing logical qubits in high-rate CSS codes using local Clifford circuits, and shows that permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is limited by code rate.
motivation: Understanding how to implement logical gates on subsets of logical qubits is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation, especially with asymptotically good codes.
method: The authors use automorphism theory of CSS codes and combinatorial arguments to derive no-go theorems for addressability under fault-tolerant constraints.
result: For CSS codes with non-zero rate, one cannot address logical X, Z, H, or S gates to a strict subset of logical qubits using 1-local Clifford circuits; also, permuting logical qubits via physical permutations is impossible if rate > 1/3 and distance ≥ 3.
conclusion: There is a fundamental trade-off between addressability and code efficiency, which must be considered for practical quantum computation.

title: Query And Depth Upper Bounds For Quantum Unitaries Via Grover Search
authors: Gregory Rosenthal
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2144 (2026).

We prove that any [MATH]-qubit unitary can be implemented (i) approximately in time [MATH] with query access to an appropriate classical oracle, and also (ii) exactly by a circuit of depth [MATH] with one- and two-qubit gates and [MATH] ancillae. The proofs involve similar reductions to Grover search. The proof of (ii) also involves a linear-depth construction of arbitrary quantum states using one- and two-qubit gates (in fact, this can be improved to constant depth with the addition of fanout and generalized Toffoli gates) which may be of independent interest. We also prove a matching [MATH] lower bound for (i) and (ii) for a certain class of implementations.

.
tldr: This paper proves upper and lower bounds on query complexity and circuit depth for implementing arbitrary quantum unitaries using Grover search.
motivation: Understanding the minimal resources (queries, depth) needed to implement arbitrary quantum operations is fundamental to quantum computing and information theory.
method: The authors reduce unitary implementation to Grover search, constructing circuits with linear depth and ancillae, and prove matching lower bounds for a class of implementations.
result: Any n-qubit unitary can be implemented approximately in time O(2^{n/2}) with query access to a classical oracle, and exactly by a circuit of depth O(2^{n/2}) with one- and two-qubit gates and O(2^{n/2}) ancillae. A matching lower bound is also shown.
conclusion: The results provide tight resource bounds for unitary synthesis, highlighting the power of Grover search in quantum circuit design.

title: Saturation Attack Of The Microwave-propagated Continuous Variable Quantum Key Distribution In Open Air
authors: Wenqi Peng, Xuan Li, Yongxin Feng, Xiu-Bo Chen And Ying Guo
abstract: Continuous variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) can achieve the secure communication between two distant legitimate users. The microwave CVQKD exhibits stronger robustness than the optical CVQKD in transmitting quantum signals and accordingly has broad application prospects in quantum networks. Although the microwave CVQKD does not rely on the traditional optical fibers to transmit quantum signals, its practical security is still vulnerable to saturation attacks. In view of this security vulnerability, we generalize saturation attacks to microwave CVQKD and clarify the impact of saturation attacks on the parameter estimation of microwave systems. Two saturation attack schemes are further compared, one based on displacement control alone and the other on joint displacement and gain control. To mitigate the negative impacts caused by this attack, we propose a countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm, which can detect saturation attacks by measuring unknown quantum states. In addition, the influence of microwave antennas on the security of the communication system is assessed, confirming that antenna gain plays a key role in determining both the secret key rate and the maximum transmission distance.
tldr: This paper generalizes saturation attacks to microwave continuous-variable QKD and proposes a countermeasure using quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
motivation: Microwave CVQKD offers robust quantum signal transmission but is vulnerable to saturation attacks; the paper aims to analyze and mitigate this security threat.
method: The authors model two saturation attack schemes (displacement control alone vs. joint displacement and gain control) and propose a detection countermeasure based on the quantum nearest neighbor algorithm.
result: The analysis shows that antenna gain critically affects secret key rate and maximum transmission distance, and the proposed countermeasure can detect saturation attacks.
conclusion: Saturation attacks pose a practical security risk to microwave CVQKD, but can be mitigated by the proposed detection method, enhancing the security of quantum networks.

title: Capturing An Electron In The Virtual State
authors: Alok Nath Singh, Bibek Bhandari, Rafael Sánchez And Andrew N Jordan
abstract: We address a foundational question in quantum mechanics: can a particle be directly found in a classically-forbidden virtual state? We instantiate this conceptual question by investigating the traversal of electrons through a tunnel barrier, which we define in a triple quantum dot system where the occupation of the central dot is energetically avoided. The motivation behind this setup is to answer whether the central dot is occupied or not during a virtual transition when it is being explicitly monitored. We investigate this problem in two different limits of continuous measurements: the stochastic quantum diffusion and the quantum jump. We find that, even though individual trajectories differ considerably across these limits, measuring leads to a higher occupation in the central dot on average. We also find that a suitably strong measurement can significantly boost the tunneling current—an effect we call measurement-assisted tunneling. Our results demonstrate that the act of observation fundamentally reshapes tunneling dynamics, resolving the seeming paradox of detecting a particle in a classically forbidden region: weak measurements partially localize the particle, while strong measurements enforce a discontinuous either/or detection or no detection outcome.
tldr: This paper investigates whether an electron can be detected in a classically forbidden virtual state by monitoring a triple quantum dot system, revealing measurement-assisted tunneling.
motivation: To resolve the foundational question of whether a particle can be found in a virtual state during a tunneling process, and to understand the role of continuous measurement in quantum dynamics.
method: The authors model a triple quantum dot system with energetically forbidden central dot occupation and analyze two continuous measurement limits: stochastic quantum diffusion and quantum jumps.
result: Measurements increase the average occupation of the central dot, and strong measurements can significantly boost tunneling current, an effect termed measurement-assisted tunneling.
conclusion: The act of observation reshapes tunneling dynamics, with weak measurements partially localizing the particle and strong measurements enforcing discontinuous detection outcomes.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A temporal coarse-graining method for simulating classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, with practical advantages for noise with multiple time scales.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with classical stochastic noise that has temporal correlations over many time scales (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging. The authors aim to develop an efficient simulation approach.
method: The method performs temporal coarse-graining by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization, expressing it as a sum of deterministic functions and bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the bridge processes are independent and have analytically known correlators, allowing precomputation of noise propagators.
result: The approach yields a simple concatenation rule and numerical examples demonstrate its practical advantages for simulating noise with multiple time scales.
conclusion: The temporal coarse-graining method provides an efficient way to simulate quantum systems under classical stochastic noise, particularly useful for solid-state quantum information processors where 1/f noise is prevalent.

title: Steady-state Entanglement Harvesting For Two Rotating Atoms In A Cylindrical Cavity
authors: Hong-Tao Zheng, Xiang-Fa Zhou, Guang-Can Guo And Zheng-Wei Zhou
abstract: We study the entanglement dynamics of two rotating atoms (with two internal levels and ) in a cylindrical cavity, which interact with a massless scalar field in vacuum satisfying the Dirichlet boundary condition. Our analysis demonstrates that it is possible to obtain the steady-state entanglement under two types of resonant conditions. For two identical atoms with the same world-line, the system reduces to the usual dissipative Dicke model at the first resonant condition where and are the energy splitting and the angular velocity of the th atom, and is the Lorentz factor. The entangled steady-state takes the form where and are constant, which is consistent with the previous study (see 2022 Phys. Rev. D 106 105028). For two atoms with different world-lines, the system suffers from a significant mixed joint dissipation process at the second resonant condition , and reaches an entangled steady-state as . Moreover, with the help of the cavity, we can obtain a much higher concurrence in the final states by changing the relative ratio of the two orbital radii. Our work thus provides a more effective way for the extraction of steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect for two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity.
tldr: Two rotating atoms in a cylindrical cavity can harvest steady-state entanglement from the vacuum via the analogue Unruh effect.
motivation: To study entanglement dynamics and steady-state entanglement harvesting for rotating atoms in a cavity, which is relevant to understanding quantum information in non-inertial frames and curved spacetimes.
method: The authors model two two-level atoms rotating in a cylindrical cavity with Dirichlet boundary conditions, interacting with a massless scalar field. They derive master equations and analyze resonant conditions for steady-state entanglement.
result: Steady-state entanglement is achievable under two resonant conditions, with higher concurrence obtained by tuning the orbital radii ratio. The system reduces to the dissipative Dicke model for identical world-lines.
conclusion: The work provides an effective method for extracting steady-state entanglement from vacuum using rotating atoms in a cavity, with potential applications in quantum information processing.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a near-optimal parameter tuning method for level-1 QAOA on Ising models, reducing the optimization to a structured signal-processing problem.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, even for shallow circuits; the authors aim to show that tuning is not a black-box search but a structured problem.
method: They prove the QAOA1 expectation is a partial Fourier series, derive instance-wise bandwidth bounds, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization.
result: The method achieves polynomial-time global optimization with optimality certificates for commensurable weights, and validates on RQAOA for 128- and 256-qubit weighted instances, outperforming coarse optimization and SDP.
conclusion: Parameter tuning for shallow QAOA can be solved efficiently by exploiting its Fourier structure, enabling better performance in recursive QAOA.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.
