tldr: This paper studies the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations needed to prepare graph states, establishing a combinatorial characterization and relating it to rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of graph-state preparation is important for quantum computing and communication, as graph states are a key resource.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and elementary edge-complementations.
result: They show that CZ-complexity is bounded by O(rw(G)^2) and at least Ω(rw(G)) for connected graphs, and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
conclusion: The work provides tight bounds on the complexity of graph-state preparation, but the topic is not a core focus of the user's interests.

title: Exact Quantum Many-Body Scars In 2d Quantum Gauge Models
authors: Yuan Miao, Linhao Li, Hosho Katsura, And Masahito Yamazaki
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2164 (2026).

Quantum many-body scars (QMBS) serve as important examples of ergodicity-breaking phenomena in quantum many-body systems. Despite recent extensive studies, exact QMBS are rare in dimensions higher than one. In this paper, we study a two-dimensional quantum [MATH] gauge model that is dual to a two-dimensional spin-[MATH] XY model defined on bipartite graphs. We identify the exact eigenstates of the XY model with a tower structure as exact QMBS. Exploiting the duality transformation, we show that the exact QMBS of the XY model (and XXZ model) after the transformation are the exact QMBS of the dual [MATH] gauge model. This construction is versatile and has potential applications for finding new QMBS in other higher-dimensional models.

.
tldr: This paper constructs exact quantum many-body scars in a 2D quantum gauge model via duality to an XY model.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are rare in higher dimensions; the authors aim to provide exact examples in 2D gauge theories.
method: They identify exact eigenstates with a tower structure in a 2D spin-1/2 XY model on bipartite graphs, then use a duality transformation to map them to exact scars in the dual U(1) gauge model.
result: Exact QMBS are found in both the XY model and the dual gauge model, demonstrating a versatile construction for higher-dimensional scars.
conclusion: This work provides a new class of exact QMBS in 2D, with potential for generalization to other models.

title: Pseudo-Hermitian Magnon Dynamics
authors: Xi-Guang Wang And Jamal Berakdar
abstract: A defining quantity of a physical system is its energy which is represented by the Hamiltonian. In closed quantum mechanical or/and fully coherent wave-based systems the Hamiltonian is introduced as a Hermitian operator which ensures real energy spectrum and secures the decomposition of any state over a complete basis set that spans the space where states live. Pseudo-Hermitian, or PT symmetric, systems are a special class of non-Hermitian ones. They describe open systems but may still have real energy spectrum. The eigenmodes are however not orthogonal in general. This qualitative difference to Hermitian physics has a range of consequences for the physical behavior of the system in the steady state or when it is subjected to external perturbations. This overview reviews the recent progress in the field of pseudo-Hermitian physics as it unfolds when applied to low-energy excitations of magnetically ordered materials. The focus is mainly on long wavelength spin excitations (spin waves) with magnons being the energy quanta of these excitations. Various setups including ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with different types of coupling to the environments as well as spatio-temporally engineered systems will be discussed with a focus on the particular aspects that are brought about by the pseudo-Hermiticity such as mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, PT-symmetric assisted Floquet engineering, topological energy transfer, and field-induced enhanced sensitivity.
tldr: A review of pseudo-Hermitian magnon dynamics in magnetically ordered materials, focusing on non-Hermitian effects such as mode amplification and non-reciprocal propagation.
motivation: To understand how pseudo-Hermiticity (PT symmetry) modifies the behavior of magnons in various magnetic systems, potentially enabling novel functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental progress on pseudo-Hermitian magnonics, covering ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, magnonic crystals, and hybrid structures with environmental coupling.
result: Pseudo-Hermitian magnon systems exhibit unique phenomena like mode amplification, non-reciprocal propagation, magnon cloaking, non-Hermitian skin effect, and PT-symmetric Floquet engineering.
conclusion: Pseudo-Hermitian magnonics is a rapidly developing field with potential for novel wave-based devices, but the review does not present new results or directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Green’s Function Methods For Computing Supercurrents In Josephson Junctions
authors: Eduardo R Mucciolo, Jouko Nieminen, Xiao Xiao, Wei-Chi Chiu, Michael N Leuenberger And Arun Bansil
abstract: Interest in Josephson junctions (JJs) has increased rapidly in recent years not only because of their use in qubits and other quantum devices but also due to the unique physics supported by the JJs. The advent of various novel quantum materials for both the barrier region and the superconducting leads has led to the possibility of adding new functionalities to the JJs. Thus, there is a growing need for accurate modeling of the JJs and related systems to enable their predictive control and atomistic level understanding. This review presents an in-depth discussion of a Green’s-function-based formalism for computing supercurrents in JJs. The formulation is tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations and encompasses both dc and ac supercurrents. We hope that this review will provide a timely and comprehensive reference for researchers as well as beginning practitioners interested in Green’s-function-based methods to model supercurrents in JJs.
tldr: A review of Green's function methods for computing supercurrents in Josephson junctions, focusing on large-scale atomistic simulations.
motivation: Josephson junctions are key components in qubits and quantum devices, and accurate modeling is needed for predictive control and atomistic understanding.
method: The paper presents a Green's-function-based formalism tailored for large-scale atomistic simulations to compute both dc and ac supercurrents.
result: The formalism enables accurate modeling of supercurrents in Josephson junctions with novel quantum materials.
conclusion: This review provides a comprehensive reference for researchers interested in Green's-function-based modeling of supercurrents in JJs.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting to build zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks, with applications to NP and QMA.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on commitments not known from standard assumptions; this work aims to provide such protocols from the LWE assumption.
method: The authors extend the MPC-in-the-head technique to quantum computations, constructing three-round zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA in the common reference string model.
result: They obtain zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA secure against superposition attacks, with security based on the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem.
conclusion: This work provides the first zero-knowledge protocols for NP and QMA with superposition security from standard cryptographic assumptions, advancing quantum cryptography.

title: Machine Learning Decoding Of Circuit-Level Noise For Bivariate Bicycle Codes
authors: John Blue, Harshil Avlani, Zhiyang He, Liu Ziyin, And Isaac L. Chuang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2149 (2026).

Fault-tolerant quantum computers will depend crucially on the performance of the classical decoding algorithm which takes in the results of measurements and outputs corrections to the errors inferred to have occurred. Machine learning models have shown great promise as decoders for the surface code; however, this promise has not yet been substantiated for the more challenging task of decoding quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes. In this paper, we present a recurrent, transformer-based neural network designed to decode circuit-level noise on Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. For the [MATH] BB code, at a physical error rate of [MATH], our model achieves logical error rates almost [MATH] times lower than belief propagation with ordered statistics decoding (BP-OSD), and roughly [MATH] times larger than a most-likely error decoder. Moreover, while BP-OSD has a wide distribution of runtimes with significant outliers, our model has a consistent runtime and is an order-of-magnitude faster than the worst-case times from a benchmark BP-OSD implementation. On the [MATH] BB code, our model obtains worse logical error rates but maintains the speed advantage. These results provide initial evidence that machine learning decoders can out-perform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but suggest more complex architectures and/or training procedures are necessary to scale to larger code sizes.

.
tldr: This paper applies machine learning decoding to bivariate bicycle codes, a type of quantum LDPC code, achieving lower logical error rates than BP-OSD on small codes but not scaling well.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires efficient decoders for quantum LDPC codes, which are more challenging than surface codes. Machine learning decoders have shown promise for surface codes but not yet for QLDPC codes.
method: A recurrent, transformer-based neural network is designed to decode circuit-level noise on bivariate bicycle codes. The model is trained and tested on small BB codes and compared to BP-OSD and most-likely error decoders.
result: On the [72,12,6] BB code, the ML decoder achieves logical error rates almost 10 times lower than BP-OSD and roughly 2 times larger than a most-likely error decoder, with consistent runtime an order-of-magnitude faster. On a larger code, error rates are worse but speed advantage remains.
conclusion: Machine learning decoders can outperform conventional decoders on small QLDPC codes, but scaling to larger codes requires more complex architectures or training procedures.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory but can be reproduced classically, and relates it to broader foundational puzzles.
motivation: To challenge the view that Wigner's Friend highlights a uniquely quantum feature and to show its relevance to other foundational problems.
method: The authors construct classical thought experiments that mimic extended Wigner's Friend scenarios and identify a common structural feature called 'Restriction A'.
result: Classical scenarios can reproduce some implications of the paradox, and the same structural difficulty underlies puzzles like the Boltzmann brain problem.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing issues of private versus intersubjective verification.

title: Observation Of Alignment Tensor Effects In Metastability-exchange Collisions With Highly Polarized 3 ...
authors: Yida Sha, Kaiwen Yi, Xingqing Jin, Matteo Fadel And Xiang Peng
abstract: Highly polarized ensembles prepared by metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) have been widely used in precision measurements and fundamental physics. Metastability-exchange (ME) collisions, serving as the basis of MEOP, are traditionally described in terms of atomic orientation, while the significant contributions of metastable alignment tensor at high polarization remain unexplored. In this work, we develop a linearized model under mean-field approximation to investigate alignment tensor effects in highly polarized , which originate from the metastable manifold and are revealed through ME-induced relaxation and frequency shift. By means of free-induction-decay measurements, a pronounced dependence on nuclear polarization is experimentally observed in the response of the ground-state-metastable hybrid ensembles to the external magnetic field. Furthermore, after obtaining the characteristics of tensor-induced phenomena, we demonstrate good agreement between the experiment and the theory. This work advances the understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized using MEOP. It further provides applications in systematic error correction of high-accuracy magnetometry, as well as in optimal protocol for the generation of nuclear spin-squeezed states.
tldr: This paper studies alignment tensor effects in metastability-exchange collisions with highly polarized 3He, focusing on nuclear spin dynamics and magnetometry applications.
motivation: To understand alignment tensor contributions in highly polarized 3He ensembles, which are not captured by traditional orientation-based models, and to improve precision measurements.
method: Develops a linearized mean-field model and validates it with free-induction-decay measurements on metastability-exchange optical pumping (MEOP) ensembles.
result: Observes a pronounced dependence of the ground-state-metastable hybrid ensemble response on nuclear polarization, and achieves good agreement between theory and experiment.
conclusion: Advances understanding of nuclear spin dynamics in highly polarized 3He and provides applications for systematic error correction in magnetometry and generation of spin-squeezed states.

title: Parity-mixing Interference In Laser-assisted Photoionization
authors: N Ouahioune, D Hoff, P K Maroju, C L Arnold, D Busto, A L’huillier, M Gisselbrecht And S Carlström
abstract: Photoionization of atoms by high-order harmonics in the presence of a laser may lead to quantum interference from which information about the photoionization dynamics or the light fields can be extracted. Traditionally, this interference arises from two-photon transitions involving the absorption of consecutive harmonics combined with the absorption and stimulated emission of a laser photon. In this process, parity is conserved. Here, we investigate interference between one- and two-photon transitions in helium using high-order harmonics generated by a few-cycle laser and three-dimensional electron detection. In this case, parity is not conserved. We identify four parity-mixing interference pathways, involving two different harmonic fields or a single harmonic, together with absorption or emission of a probe photon.
tldr: This paper studies parity-mixing interference in laser-assisted photoionization of helium, a topic in atomic physics and ultrafast optics.
motivation: To understand quantum interference pathways that violate parity conservation in photoionization, which can reveal information about photoionization dynamics or light fields.
method: High-order harmonics generated by a few-cycle laser are used to ionize helium, and three-dimensional electron detection is employed to identify interference pathways.
result: Four parity-mixing interference pathways are identified, involving one- and two-photon transitions with different harmonic fields and probe photon absorption/emission.
conclusion: Parity-mixing interference provides a new tool for probing photoionization dynamics and characterizing light fields.

title: Strain-driven Transition From Correlated Insulating To Semimetallic States In Twisted-bilayer Graphene
authors: Lishuai Guo, Abulimiti Yasen, Mei Xiang, Wenliang Zhu And Minghu Pan
abstract: We investigate the interplay between Coulomb interaction and uniaxial heterostrain in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) using a self-consistent Hartree–Fock (HF) approach projected onto the flat bands. For integer filling factors in the range of , we find that heterostrain strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure and suppresses interaction-induced insulating gaps. As strain magnitude increases, the flat-band bandwidth is substantially enhanced, leading to an increased kinetic energy. The bandwidth enhancement effectively weakens the interaction strength relative to kinetic energy, resulting in the suppression of HF gaps and the emergence of semimetallic (SM) states. The strain effect can be primarily controlled by the filling factor, as well as the strain direction. At moderate strain strengths around 0.3% for , it can drive transitions between correlated insulating and SM states. In contrast, for , the HF gaps becomes negligible and the system remains essentially SM; both the strain direction and magnitude have negligible influence. Our results demonstrate that uniaxial heterostrain serves as an effective and versatile parameter for tuning correlated phases in TBG through the interplay of lattice deformation and Coulomb interactions.
tldr: This paper studies strain-driven transitions between correlated insulating and semimetallic states in twisted bilayer graphene using Hartree-Fock calculations.
motivation: Understanding how uniaxial heterostrain affects correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene, which is a key material in condensed matter physics.
method: Self-consistent Hartree-Fock approach projected onto flat bands to compute band structure and interaction-induced gaps under varying strain.
result: Heterostrain enhances bandwidth, suppresses insulating gaps, and drives transitions to semimetallic states; effect depends on filling factor and strain direction.
conclusion: Uniaxial heterostrain is an effective tuning parameter for correlated phases in twisted bilayer graphene.

title: Observation Of Floquet Tensor Monopoles
authors: Hao Yuan, Weixuan Zhang, Na Sun And Xiangdong Zhang
abstract: Tensor monopoles, topological singularities of Kalb–Ramond tensor gauge fields, have garnered widespread attention in high-energy and condensed matter physics. They give rise to exotic phenomena such as quantized magnetoelectric responses and chiral boundary states, acting as potential building blocks for the development of topological devices in high-dimensional space. However, theoretical studies and experimental realizations reported to date have remained in static settings, and the realization of Floquet tensor monopoles (FTMs) and their associated anomalous non-equilibrium topological features has yet to be achieved. Here, we report the first theoretical and experimental implementation of FTMs in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system. We systematically uncover the driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of FTMs, together with their anomalous bulk-edge correspondence. These phenomena are unique to FTMs and have no static counterparts. In experiments, we design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits, and directly observe the controllable motion of FTMs in k-space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency. Our findings extend tensor monopole research to the non-equilibrium regime, providing a theoretical and experimental platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and laying the groundwork for functional topological devices with real-time control.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of Floquet tensor monopoles in a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, demonstrating controllable creation, motion, and annihilation of tensor monopoles and their anomalous bulk-edge correspondence.
motivation: Tensor monopoles have been studied in static settings, but their non-equilibrium (Floquet) counterparts and associated topological features have not been realized experimentally.
method: The authors design and fabricate time-varying topological circuits to realize a four-dimensional non-equilibrium system, and observe the motion of Floquet tensor monopoles in momentum space and their induced 3D Fermi-arc surface states by tuning the driving frequency.
result: They observe driving-frequency controlled creation, motion, and annihilation of Floquet tensor monopoles, along with anomalous bulk-edge correspondence unique to the non-equilibrium regime.
conclusion: This work extends tensor monopole research to non-equilibrium systems, providing a platform for exploring exotic topological phases in dynamic tensor gauge fields and potential topological devices with real-time control.

title: A Less-for-more Metamaterial Paradigm Via Laplace-Helmholtz Correspondence
authors: Zihang Guo, Fubao Yang, Tong Li, Shuihua Yang, Cheng-Wei Qiu, Jingjing He And Liujun Xu
abstract: The Laplace and Helmholtz equations dominate two fundamentally distinct physical processes: steady diffusion with a single constitutive parameter versus dynamic wave propagation with two. Manipulating complex wave dynamics through simple steady fields is typically deemed infeasible. Here, we bridge this gap by establishing the Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence, enabling a ‘less-for-more’ paradigm for metamaterial design. Rooted in a wave invariant, this framework allows the rigorous derivation of the two parameters and oscillatory field for the Helmholtz equation (the ‘more’) solely from the single parameter and steady field of the Laplace equation (the ‘less’). We demonstrate this capability by unlocking functionalities previously considered intractable, such as hyperbolic invisibility and three-dimensional freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance. We further experimentally validate our strategy via a waveguide cloak. Our results bridge static and dynamic physics, establishing a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints.
tldr: This paper establishes a mathematical correspondence between Laplace and Helmholtz equations to design metamaterials for wave manipulation using static diffusion fields.
motivation: To bridge the gap between static diffusion and dynamic wave physics, enabling simpler design of complex wave functionalities.
method: The authors derive a wave invariant that maps the single-parameter Laplace equation to the two-parameter Helmholtz equation, allowing wave fields to be obtained from steady-state solutions.
result: They demonstrate hyperbolic invisibility and 3D freeform conformal cloaking with broadband performance, and experimentally validate a waveguide cloak.
conclusion: The Laplace-Helmholtz correspondence provides a versatile gateway for manipulating waves beyond conventional constraints, but the work is focused on metamaterial design and wave physics, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Comprehensive Review On Master Stability Functions In Complex Network Dynamics
authors: Priodyuti Pradhan And Chandrakala Meena Suman Acharyya
abstract: Synchronization is a fundamental emergent phenomenon observed across a wide range of natural and engineered systems. Understanding the stability of a synchronization phenomenon is crucial for ensuring functionality in various complex systems. The master stability function (MSF) framework has emerged as a powerful and elegant tool for analyzing the stability of synchronization in coupled dynamical systems. By separating the effects of the node dynamics from the network structure, the MSF offers deep insights into synchronization behavior. However, a major challenge lies in determining the MSF for complex dynamical networks driven by nonlinear interaction mechanisms. These mechanisms introduce additional complexity due to the intricate connectivity of the interacting elements and the complex dynamics governed by nonlinear processes, diverse parameters, and the higher dimensionality of the system. Although MSF analysis has been widely used for more than past 25 years, a comprehensive and systematic investigation of MSF across various networked systems is still lacking. In this article, we present a simplified and unified analysis for the MSF in various undirected and directed networked systems. We begin by formulating the MSF framework in pairwise coupled identical systems and extend our analysis to directed networks and multilayer networks, considering both intralayer and interlayer interactions. Furthermore, we analyze the MSF formalism for higher-order networks. To facilitate understanding, we complement the theoretical developments with numerical analysis of synchronization stability in coupled systems. We also propose algorithms for computing the MSF, identifying stability regimes, and classifying the MSF behaviors. Overall, the primary goal of this review is to present a systematic study of the MSF in various coupled dynamical networks in a clear and structured manner, making this powerful tool more accessible. Furthermore, we highlight underexplored areas in the application of the MSF and discuss emerging directions, such as estimating the MSF using machine learning approaches.
tldr: A comprehensive review of the master stability function framework for analyzing synchronization stability in complex networks, covering pairwise, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks.
motivation: Synchronization is a key emergent phenomenon in natural and engineered systems, and understanding its stability is crucial. The master stability function (MSF) is a powerful tool, but a systematic review across various network types is lacking.
method: The paper formulates the MSF framework for pairwise coupled identical systems, extends it to directed and multilayer networks with intralayer and interlayer interactions, and analyzes higher-order networks. Numerical simulations and algorithms for computing MSF are provided.
result: A unified and simplified MSF analysis is presented for undirected, directed, multilayer, and higher-order networks, along with algorithms to compute MSF and classify stability regimes.
conclusion: The review systematically organizes MSF theory across diverse network types, making the tool more accessible, and highlights underexplored areas and future directions such as machine learning-based MSF estimation.

title: Classification And Correlation Signatures Of Chiral Spin Liquids On The Pyrochlore Lattice
authors: Leon Balents And Yasir Iqbal Chunxiao Liu
abstract: We present a systematic classification and variational study of chiral quantum spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice based on fermionic parton constructions. Focusing on chiral and spin-liquid Ansätze, we characterize their symmetry properties, flux structures, and low-energy spinon spectra within a projective symmetry group framework, and incorporate gauge fluctuations through Gutzwiller-projected wave functions studied by variational Monte Carlo. From the equal-time spin structure factor, we develop correlation-based diagnostics that distinguish gauge-dominated Coulomb phases from states with substantial matter-field and short-range contributions. Distinct chiral flux sectors, though close in energy, exhibit markedly different degrees of emergent gauge-field dominance, reflected in the geometry and contrast of pinch-point singularities. Although these states are not competitive ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model, they define a physically meaningful family of proximate chiral phases relevant to extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians.
tldr: This paper classifies chiral spin liquids on the pyrochlore lattice using parton constructions and variational Monte Carlo, focusing on symmetry and flux structures.
motivation: Chiral spin liquids are exotic quantum phases with potential relevance to frustrated magnetism, but the paper's focus is on classification and correlation signatures rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use fermionic parton constructions, projective symmetry group analysis, and Gutzwiller-projected wave functions studied by variational Monte Carlo.
result: They identify distinct chiral flux sectors with different degrees of gauge-field dominance, reflected in pinch-point singularities of the spin structure factor.
conclusion: These chiral phases are not ground states of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model but are relevant to extended pyrochlore Hamiltonians.

title: Physical Sampling For Computational Photography
authors: Ni Chen And David J Brady
abstract: The standard model of photography is that lenses form images and focal planes capture those images. Over the past two decades, however, cameras have been transformed from devices that record focal images into analog-to-digital converters that transform massively parallel optical signals into serial electronic data. Under this new model, one may choose to maximize the quality and quantity of captured information, rather than focal image quality. Here we review the nature of the optical data stream and consider lens and focal plane designs that improve information capture capacity. After maximizing information capacity, the challenge of converting this information to digital data requires novel read-out and compression. We review strategies for approaching physical information limits under realistic size, power, and bandwidth constraints. Multiscale monocentric (spherical primary optics combined with arrays of secondary micro-cameras, each imaging a narrow subfield) and array lens architectures relax unfavorable geometric scaling by trading monolithic optics for co-designed system-level integration (jointly optimized optics, focal-plane, and readout subsystems). Metaoptic and mode-sorting focal plane filters implement richer projection operators that sample spectral, polarimetric, and coherence features without requiring exhaustive scanning. Finally, because readout and computation dominate energy at high throughput, we highlight architectures that perform dimensionality reduction before (or during) digitization, including integrated photonic encoders and multilayer optical projections coupled to detection and learned decoding. Together, these developments motivate a shift from cameras optimized to produce 2D images toward cameras engineered as end-to-end information channels, co-designing optics, focal-plane, and readout to deliver more task-relevant measurements per photon and per joule.
tldr: This paper reviews computational photography as an information channel, focusing on optical sampling and readout architectures to maximize information capture under physical constraints.
motivation: Traditional cameras are limited by geometric scaling and bandwidth; the authors aim to redesign cameras as end-to-end information channels to improve information capacity per photon and per joule.
method: The paper surveys multiscale monocentric optics, metaoptic filters, and integrated photonic encoders that perform dimensionality reduction before digitization, co-designing optics, focal plane, and readout.
result: The review identifies architectures that relax unfavorable scaling and improve information capture, but does not present novel experimental or theoretical results.
conclusion: Future cameras should be engineered as information channels, co-optimizing all subsystems to deliver more task-relevant measurements under size, power, and bandwidth constraints.

title: Rashba-like Spin Splitting In Inversion Symmetric Plasmonic Metasurface
authors: Sujit Rajak, Nishkarsh Kumar, Dheeraj Yadav, Suman Mandal, Jeeban K Nayak, Ayan Banerjee, Subhasish Dutta Gupta, Olivier Martin And Nirmalya Ghosh
abstract: Spin-dependent dispersion and Rashba effect are manifestations of spin–orbit interaction (SOI) associated with the breaking of the spatial inversion symmetry in condensed matter and in optical systems. Here, we report an extraordinary spin-split dispersion effect of leaky surface plasmons in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic crystal. Momentum domain polarization analysis identified a transverse momentum-dependent linear birefringence–linear dichroism (geometric LB–LD) effect responsible for this phenomena. It is demonstrated that evolution of strong geometrical phase gradient due to the geometric LB–LD effect mediates the spin-split dispersion in inversion symmetric plasmonic metasurface through spin (circular polarization)-dependent transverse momentum. This unconventional SOI phenomena offers a new paradigm of spin-based dispersion engineering and spin-controlled nano-optical functionalities by encompassing the forbidden class of symmetric metastructures in the realm of spin optics.
tldr: This paper reports a Rashba-like spin splitting effect in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic metasurface, mediated by geometric phase gradients.
motivation: To demonstrate spin-dependent dispersion in systems with inversion symmetry, which is typically forbidden, and to explore new paradigms for spin-controlled nano-optics.
method: Momentum domain polarization analysis is used to identify a transverse momentum-dependent linear birefringence–linear dichroism (geometric LB–LD) effect, and the evolution of geometric phase gradients is analyzed.
result: A spin-split dispersion of leaky surface plasmons is observed in an inversion-symmetric plasmonic crystal, arising from the geometric LB–LD effect.
conclusion: This unconventional spin-orbit interaction phenomenon enables spin-based dispersion engineering and spin-controlled nano-optical functionalities in symmetric metastructures.

title: Machine-learning-enabled Solvent Engineering For Uniform Quantum Dot Packing In Efficient And Stable Quantum-dot Light-emitting Diodes
authors: Beomsoo Chun, Byong Jae Kim, Hyeongjin Kim, Jeong Han Song, Yeongsik Kim, Jaehoon Lim And Jeonghun Kwak
abstract: Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) offer size-tunable optoelectronic properties and solution processability, yet achieving uniformly packed emissive layers remains a bottleneck for high-performance quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs). Here, we report a machine learning -guided solvent optimization strategy to produce homogeneous QD films. Five representative solvent parameters are evaluated, and multiple regression models are trained against film uniformity derived from atomic force microscopy. Among them, support vector regression provides the highest predictive accuracy for film homogeneity. Guided by these predictions, we formulate a mixed solvent that closely matches the target profile, yielding superior packing homogeneity, which is confirmed by grazing-incidence small-angle x-ray scattering. QLEDs fabricated with this formulation exhibit an external quantum efficiency of 20.6% and an operational lifetime of 468.5 h at 20 000 cd m−2, surpassing all single-solvent controls. These findings establish packing homogeneity as a decisive factor for device performance and introduce a generalizable and scalable framework for data-driven design of solution-processed devices, holding strong potential for next-generation optoelectronic systems.
tldr: This paper uses machine learning to optimize solvent mixtures for uniform quantum dot packing in QLEDs, achieving high efficiency and long lifetime.
motivation: Achieving uniformly packed emissive layers is a bottleneck for high-performance quantum-dot light-emitting diodes (QLEDs).
method: Five solvent parameters were evaluated, and multiple regression models (with support vector regression best) were trained to predict film uniformity from atomic force microscopy data, guiding the formulation of a mixed solvent.
result: The optimized solvent yielded superior packing homogeneity, and QLEDs achieved 20.6% external quantum efficiency and 468.5 h operational lifetime at 20,000 cd/m².
conclusion: Packing homogeneity is a decisive factor for device performance, and the data-driven framework is generalizable for solution-processed devices.

In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. title: Decoupling Local Classicality From Classical Explainability: A Noncontextual Model For Bilocal Classical Theory And A Locally-classical But Contextual Theory
authors: Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, And John H.selby
abstract:

We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [1]. To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from [1] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in [2] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens' toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.
